title: Valvular Heart Diseases
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)

overview.intro: This chapter explains how diseases of the heart valves change the load on the chambers around them and how those loads produce the murmurs, pulses, and symptoms that identify each lesion. It covers the four left-sided lesions, infective and sterile endocarditis, mitral valve prolapse, chronic rheumatic heart disease, carcinoid heart disease, and prosthetic valve complications. One principle runs through all of it: a stenotic valve imposes a pressure load on the chamber behind it, a regurgitant valve imposes a volume load, and the speed at which a lesion develops decides whether the heart can adapt. Board questions describe a murmur, pulse, maneuver, vegetation, or laboratory pattern and ask you to reason back to the lesion and its cause.
prerequisites: Pressures, volumes, and valve events of the cardiac cycle, and the origin of S1 to S4 (CV-4)
Preload, afterload, the Frank-Starling mechanism, and the law of Laplace
Acute rheumatic fever and molecular mimicry (CV-16.2)
Endocarditis organisms and their virulence factors (CV-17)
Virchow's triad and the basic steps of platelet adhesion and coagulation

connections.to: Heart valves and the cardiac cycle (CV-4)
connections.how: Every murmur in this chapter is a predictable result of the pressure differences across valves during the cardiac cycle, and the maneuver rules apply them.
Pressure overload from stenosis and volume overload from regurgitation are major causes of both diastolic and systolic heart failure.
Papillary muscle ischemia or rupture after infarction and ischemic LV dilation are leading causes of mitral regurgitation.
The bicuspid aortic valve is the most common congenital cause of early aortic stenosis, regurgitation, and endocarditis.
Endocarditis produces septic emboli, mycotic aneurysms, and immune complex disease, linking the valves to the vessels, kidneys, and skin.

terms.def: Failure of a valve to open fully, which obstructs forward flow and imposes a pressure load on the chamber behind it.
Failure of a valve to close completely, so that blood flows backward and the chambers on both sides carry an extra volume.
Thickening of the ventricular wall with a normal or small cavity, produced by adding sarcomeres in parallel in response to a pressure load.
Enlargement of the ventricular cavity with proportional wall growth, produced by adding sarcomeres in series in response to a volume load.
The difference between systolic and diastolic arterial pressure, which widens when stroke volume is large and diastolic runoff is rapid.
A weak, slowly rising, late-peaking arterial pulse characteristic of severe aortic stenosis.
A high-pitched early diastolic sound produced when fused, stiff mitral leaflets dome open in mitral stenosis.
Joining of adjacent valve leaflets at their edges by scar tissue, the hallmark of rheumatic valve disease.
Accumulation of proteoglycan in the spongiosa with weakening of the collagenous fibrosa, producing floppy, redundant leaflets.
A mass of platelets and fibrin, with or without organisms and inflammatory cells, attached to the endocardium or a valve.
Small sterile fibrin-platelet vegetations on the lines of closure of normal valves, arising in hypercoagulable states such as advanced cancer.
Sterile vegetations on either or both surfaces of the valve leaflets in systemic lupus erythematosus.

sections.title: Aortic stenosis: causes, pressure overload, and findings

blocks.text: The normal aortic valve has three cusps and an area of about 3 to 4 cm2. Aortic stenosis (AS) is fixed narrowing at the valve, and symptoms usually appear only when the area falls to about 1 cm2 or less, so the disease progresses silently for years.

Age-related calcific AS is the most common cause in developed countries and usually presents after about age 70 on a once-normal valve. It is an active process rather than simple wear: mechanical stress injures the cusp endothelium, low-density lipoprotein and lipoprotein(a) enter the cusp, inflammation follows, and valve interstitial cells become osteoblast-like and deposit calcium. Heaped calcified masses bulge into the sinuses of Valsalva while the commissures stay unfused. The calcification is dystrophic (normal serum calcium), and the risk factors match those of atherosclerosis. A congenitally bicuspid valve (about 1 to 2% of people) concentrates stress, so the same process presents one to two decades earlier (CV-18-G.6). Rheumatic AS shows fused commissures and almost always accompanies rheumatic mitral disease (section C08).

By the law of Laplace, wall stress is proportional to pressure times radius divided by twice the wall thickness. To push a normal stroke volume through a narrow orifice the left ventricle (LV) must generate a much higher pressure, so myocytes add sarcomeres in parallel and the wall thickens around a normal cavity (concentric hypertrophy). Ejection fraction is preserved for years, but the stiff wall needs atrial contraction to fill (S4), and demand outgrows the capillaries until fibrosis and failure follow.

Angina occurs even with normal coronary arteries: demand is high, a raised LV diastolic pressure compresses subendocardial vessels, and prolonged systole shortens diastolic perfusion time. Syncope is exertional, because exercise lowers peripheral resistance while output across a fixed orifice cannot rise; a ventricular mechanoreceptor reflex and arrhythmias add to it. Dyspnea comes from high diastolic pressure transmitted to the pulmonary veins. Once symptoms appear, classic series give average survival of about 5 years after angina, 3 after syncope, and 2 after heart failure.

blocks.text: Doppler converts jet velocity (v, in m/s) to a gradient with the simplified Bernoulli equation, about 4 times v squared in mmHg. Severe AS is an area of about 1 cm2 or less, a peak velocity of about 4 m/s or more, and a mean gradient of about 40 mmHg or more. High shear unfolds von Willebrand factor multimers so that ADAMTS13 cleaves them, and the loss of large multimers favors bleeding from intestinal angiodysplasia (Heyde syndrome).

blocks.title: From Doppler velocity to wall thickness
blocks.text: An aortic jet of 4.5 m/s gives a peak gradient of 4 times 4.5 squared, about 81 mmHg, so with an arterial systolic pressure of 130 mmHg the LV must generate about 210 mmHg. By Laplace, with an unchanged radius, wall stress normalizes only if thickness rises in proportion to pressure: 210 divided by 130 is about 1.6, so a 1.0 cm wall must become about 1.6 cm thick. That wall is stiff (S4, dyspnea), hungry for oxygen while compressing its subendocardial vessels (angina), and unable to raise output during exercise (syncope).

sections.title: Aortic regurgitation: causes, volume overload, and the wide pulse pressure

blocks.text: Aortic regurgitation (AR) is diastolic backflow from the aorta into the LV, from damaged cusps (leaflet disease) or from normal cusps pulled apart by a dilated root (root disease, with its own risk of aneurysm and dissection).

Root causes include hypertension and aging; Marfan syndrome, in which mutant fibrillin-1 (FBN1) releases excess TGF-beta activity and causes cystic medial degeneration; tertiary syphilis, in which endarteritis of the vasa vasorum scars the aortic media and gives the intima a tree-bark look; ankylosing spondylitis; and ascending aortic dissection. Leaflet causes include a bicuspid valve, endocarditis that perforates a cusp, and rheumatic cusp retraction, usually with mitral disease.
Chronic AR: volume and pressure load together

The LV receives atrial inflow plus the regurgitant volume, so end-diastolic volume and, by the Frank-Starling mechanism, total stroke volume rise. Ejecting that large volume into the high-pressure aorta adds a pressure load to the volume load. Sarcomeres are added in series, the chamber dilates with proportional wall growth (eccentric hypertrophy), and chronic AR produces some of the largest ventricles seen. The dilated chamber is compliant, so diastolic pressure stays near normal and patients may be asymptomatic for years, until dilation outruns hypertrophy, contractility falls, and failure follows.
Wide pulse pressure

Systolic pressure rises with the large, rapidly ejected stroke volume, and diastolic pressure falls because the aorta empties both back into the LV and forward into vasodilated tissues (for example 170/45 mmHg). The rapid rise and collapse give bounding (water-hammer or Corrigan) pulses and named signs of the same wide pulse pressure: head bobbing (de Musset), nail bed capillary pulsation (Quincke), a pistol-shot femoral sound (Traube), and a to-and-fro femoral bruit on compression (Duroziez). The apical impulse is hyperdynamic and displaced down and laterally. Low aortic diastolic pressure also lowers coronary perfusion pressure and can cause angina.
Murmur and related sounds

The murmur is high-pitched, blowing, early diastolic, and decrescendo, starting at A2 when the gradient from aorta to LV is greatest. It is heard best at the left sternal border with the patient sitting forward in held expiration, and handgrip makes it louder by raising aortic diastolic pressure. Because regurgitation occurs only in diastole, tachycardia reduces the regurgitant volume per beat and bradycardia increases it. An Austin Flint murmur is an apical mid-to-late diastolic rumble from the regurgitant jet partly closing the anterior mitral leaflet; unlike mitral stenosis it has no opening snap or loud S1.

Acute AR (endocarditis, dissection, trauma) strikes a normal-sized, stiff LV: diastolic pressure rises steeply and may close the mitral valve early, and pulmonary edema and shock follow. Aortic and LV pressures equalize quickly, so the murmur is short and the pulse pressure is not wide (table in section C04).

sections.title: Mitral stenosis: the atrium under pressure

blocks.text: The normal mitral valve area is about 4 to 6 cm2, so left atrial (LA) and LV pressures are nearly equal in diastole. Mitral stenosis (MS) is almost always rheumatic (section C08); heavy mitral annular calcification in older adults and congenital malformations are uncommon causes.
Hemodynamics: the upstream chambers pay

Flow across an orifice varies with its area times the square root of the pressure difference. Below about 2.5 cm2 a gradient appears, and at about 1.5 cm2 or less (severe MS) LA pressure must rise substantially to fill the LV. The LA hypertrophies and dilates, while the LV downstream is underfilled, normal or small in size, with normal or low diastolic pressure. The hallmark is a pulmonary capillary wedge pressure higher than LV diastolic pressure. Hemoptysis comes from rupture of bronchial veins that connect with the congested pulmonary veins.

blocks.caption: Every chamber upstream of the narrowed valve is loaded, while the LV downstream is protected.

blocks.text: The LV fills only in diastole, and tachycardia shortens diastole more than systole, so the same volume must cross the valve at a faster rate. Because the gradient rises with the square of the flow rate, a modest rise in heart rate raises LA pressure sharply; a rise from 70 to 120 per minute can roughly double the gradient. Exercise, fever, anemia, atrial fibrillation, and pregnancy (more blood volume, output, and rate) therefore precipitate the first pulmonary edema in previously silent MS.

The stretched LA fibroses and fibrillates. Atrial fibrillation removes the atrial contribution to filling and shortens diastole, and stasis in the LA appendage forms mural thrombi that embolize to the brain, kidneys, spleen, and limbs. The enlarged LA, the most posterior chamber, can indent the esophagus (dysphagia), compress the left recurrent laryngeal nerve between the aortic arch and the LA or a dilated pulmonary artery (hoarseness, Ortner syndrome), and elevate the left main bronchus, widening the carinal angle.

blocks.predict: A patient has a narrowed mitral valve and pulmonary edema. Predict the LV end-diastolic pressure and LV size.

The edema comes from high LA and pulmonary venous pressure behind the valve, which is why wedge pressure exceeds LV diastolic pressure in MS, unlike pulmonary edema from LV failure.

sections.title: Mitral regurgitation: causes, volume overload, and the holosystolic murmur

blocks.text: Mitral competence depends on the whole apparatus: annulus, leaflets, chordae, papillary muscles, and the LV wall that holds them. Mitral regurgitation (MR) is systolic backflow into the LA from failure of any part. In primary MR the leaflets or chordae are abnormal: mitral valve prolapse (the most common primary cause in developed countries, section C07), rheumatic disease (C08), endocarditis (C05), and papillary muscle or chordal rupture. After infarction the posteromedial papillary muscle, which usually has a single arterial supply, ruptures most often (CV-18-C.6). In secondary (functional) MR a dilated LV stretches the annulus and displaces the papillary muscles, tethering normal leaflets, and the added volume dilates the LV further, so functional MR feeds itself. Ischemic papillary muscle dysfunction causes transient MR.

Because LA pressure is low, backflow starts at the onset of systole, before the aortic valve opens, so there is no true isovolumetric contraction. The regurgitant volume returns to the LV in early diastole, so both chambers are volume loaded. The LA dilates and becomes compliant, holding a large volume at modest pressure, and often fibrillates. The LV develops eccentric hypertrophy, but because it unloads into the low-pressure LA, ejection fraction overstates contractility, and a low-normal ejection fraction already signals impairment.

blocks.title: Why a normal ejection fraction misleads in MR
blocks.text: An LV in chronic MR has an end-diastolic volume of 200 mL and an end-systolic volume of 70 mL. Total stroke volume is 130 mL and ejection fraction is 65%, which looks normal. If 65 mL flows back into the LA, the regurgitant fraction (backflow as a share of total stroke volume) is 50%, and forward stroke volume is only 65 mL. If contractility declines so end-systolic volume rises to 100 mL with the same filling and regurgitant fraction, ejection fraction falls to 50% and forward stroke volume to 50 mL. A value a clinician might call low-normal reflects a ventricle that is already failing, because the low-pressure outlet flatters the ejection fraction.

The murmur is holosystolic, high-pitched, and blowing, from S1 through A2, loudest at the apex and radiating to the left axilla. Handgrip and squatting make it louder and Valsalva or standing softens it (MVP behaves differently, section C07); a ventricular septal defect murmur lies at the left lower sternal border instead. Rapid early diastolic inflow from the loaded LA produces an S3 that reflects volume rather than proving failure. S1 is soft, and early A2 widens the split of S2.

Acute MR, from papillary muscle or chordal rupture or endocarditis, fills a small, stiff LA: tall v waves on the wedge tracing, sudden pulmonary edema, and hypotension. LA pressure approaches LV pressure late in systole, so the murmur may be short, soft, or nearly absent.

sections.title: Infective endocarditis: acute versus subacute disease and its peripheral signs

blocks.text: Infective endocarditis is microbial infection of the endocardium, usually a valve, forming vegetations of platelets, fibrin, organisms, and inflammatory cells. Organisms grow inside an avascular fibrin mesh that neutrophils reach poorly, so the vegetation sheds them continuously.

Normal endothelium resists attachment. Turbulence, a scarred or congenitally abnormal valve, a prosthesis, or a catheter exposes collagen and tissue factor, and a sterile platelet-fibrin deposit forms (section C06). A transient bacteremia from chewing, dental work, procedures, injection drug use, or skin infection then seeds it. Viridans streptococci attach through adhesins and dextran, and Staphylococcus aureus binds fibrinogen and fibronectin through surface proteins such as clumping factor (CV-17.1).

blocks.title: Pathogenesis of infective endocarditis
steps: Turbulence or prior damage injures valve endothelium
Platelets and fibrin form a sterile nidus
Transient bacteremia delivers organisms
Adhesins attach organisms to the deposit
Organisms multiply under fibrin, shielded from phagocytes
Vegetation grows, destroys tissue, sheds emboli and organisms
blocks.caption: Virulent S. aureus can invade intact endothelium and skip the first two steps, which is why it infects normal valves.

blocks.text: Virulence sets the tempo. S. aureus destroys tissue and infects normal valves, causing acute endocarditis over days with high fever, rigors, large destructive vegetations, ring abscesses, and metastatic infection; skin, injection drug use, and catheters are its portals. Viridans streptococci, oral flora of low virulence, need a damaged valve (rheumatic, congenital, bicuspid, or MVP with MR) and cause subacute disease over weeks to months with low-grade fever, fatigue, weight loss, anemia, splenomegaly, and, when long-standing, clubbing. Prolonged bacteremia allows immune complexes to form, so immunologic signs dominate subacute disease. Enterococci after genitourinary or gastrointestinal procedures and Streptococcus gallolyticus with colon cancer usually follow a subacute course (CV-17.2).

Left-sided valves face higher pressures and turbulent jets, so the mitral valve is most often involved, closely followed by the aortic. In people who inject drugs the tricuspid valve is the most common site, because skin organisms and injected particles reach it first; S. aureus dominates, with Pseudomonas and Candida less often. Right-sided vegetations embolize to the lungs as multiple, often cavitating septic emboli. Left-sided fragments cause infarcts and abscesses in the brain, spleen, kidneys, and limbs and seed arterial walls as mycotic aneurysms (CV-18-K.2).

blocks.text: Continuous shedding makes bacteremia persistent, so cultures drawn at different times grow the same organism. The Duke criteria combine positive cultures and echocardiographic evidence (vegetation, abscess, new regurgitation) as major criteria with minor criteria such as a predisposing condition, fever of 38.0°C (100.4°F) or higher, and embolic or immunologic phenomena. Inflammation raises the erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein and causes anemia of chronic inflammation through hepcidin, and rheumatoid factor may be positive in subacute disease.

sections.title: Sterile vegetations: nonbacterial thrombotic and Libman-Sacks endocarditis

blocks.text: Two noninfective forms produce sterile vegetations whose main danger is embolism, not infection or valve destruction.

Nonbacterial thrombotic (marantic) endocarditis (NBTE) consists of small (about 1 to 5 mm), bland, loosely attached fibrin-platelet thrombi along the lines of closure of normal mitral and aortic leaflets, with no organisms and little inflammation. It arises when hypercoagulability meets the normal wear at the closure line. The key association is advanced malignancy, especially mucin-producing adenocarcinoma of the pancreas or lung, whose tissue factor and mucins (which engage selectins on platelets and leukocytes) also cause migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome). DIC, sepsis, antiphospholipid syndrome, and indwelling catheters are other settings. There is usually no murmur, but fragments cause infarcts in the brain, kidneys, and spleen; multiple strokes in different arterial territories in a patient with cancer are classic. An NBTE lesion can also become the nidus for infective endocarditis.

Libman-Sacks endocarditis occurs in systemic lupus erythematosus, often with antiphospholipid antibodies. Its small to medium (about 1 to 4 mm) warty vegetations can sit on either or both leaflet surfaces, including the ventricular undersurface of the mitral valve, and on the chordae and mural endocardium. They show fibrinoid necrosis with inflammation from immune complex injury (CV-16.4), and healing fibrosis deforms the leaflets, most often causing MR. Emboli and the thrombotic tendency of antiphospholipid syndrome add risk.

blocks.title: Comparison of valve vegetations
rows: Closure lines; can spread to chordae and wall

2 to 4 weeks after group A streptococcal pharyngitis
blocks.caption: Size and destruction separate infected from sterile vegetations; both leaflet surfaces point to Libman-Sacks; the clinical setting separates NBTE from rheumatic lesions.

blocks.text: Negative blood cultures do not prove a vegetation is sterile, since fastidious organisms and prior antibiotics cause culture-negative infective endocarditis. Persistent fever, valve destruction, new regurgitation, and immunologic signs favor infection, whereas cancer, lupus, or a coagulopathy with bland infarcts favors a sterile lesion.

sections.title: Mitral valve prolapse: myxomatous degeneration and the moving click

blocks.text: Mitral valve prolapse (MVP) is systolic billowing of one or both mitral leaflets above the annulus into the LA. It affects about 2 to 3% of adults and is usually asymptomatic.

The lesion is myxomatous degeneration. The spongiosa expands with proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans, and the collagen of the fibrosa becomes thin and disorganized as valve interstitial cells overproduce matrix-degrading enzymes. Leaflets become thick, redundant, and hooded between chordal attachments, the chordae elongate, thin, and may rupture, the posterior leaflet is most often involved, and the annulus may dilate. Most MVP is sporadic or familial, but heritable connective tissue disorders show the mechanism. In Marfan syndrome, deficient fibrillin-1 microfibrils fail to hold TGF-beta inactive, and excess signaling disrupts the valve matrix; in Ehlers-Danlos syndromes defective collagen weakens the fibrosa; and autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, with abnormal polycystins, is associated with MVP as well as berry aneurysms (CV-14.3).
The mid-systolic click and why maneuvers move it

As the ventricle empties in systole, the papillary muscles and annulus move closer together and the redundant leaflets lose support. At a critical LV size they billow into the LA until the slack chordae suddenly tighten, producing a sharp mid-systolic click at the apex. If coaptation then fails, a late systolic MR murmur follows the click to S2.

Anything that makes the LV smaller (standing, the strain phase of Valsalva) reaches the critical size sooner, so the click moves toward S1 and the murmur lengthens. Anything that enlarges it (squatting, passive leg raise, sustained handgrip) delays the click toward S2 and shortens the murmur. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy also worsens with a smaller ventricle, whereas the AS murmur softens. The click is systolic and moves with LV size, while the opening snap of MS is diastolic and moves with LA pressure (general maneuver physiology in CV-4.7).

Most people never develop complications; those that occur follow from the weak tissue: progressive MR as leaflets stretch, acute severe MR when a thinned chorda ruptures and leaves a flail segment, infective endocarditis on prolapsing leaflets (especially with MR), platelet-fibrin thrombi on the atrial surface that embolize and cause transient ischemic attacks or stroke, and atrial and ventricular arrhythmias linked to papillary muscle traction and adjacent fibrosis. Sudden cardiac death is rare.

blocks.predict: A patient with MVP squats from standing. Predict the timing of the click and the length of the murmur.
blocks.explain: The click moves later toward S2 and the murmur shortens. Squatting raises venous return and afterload, so the LV stays larger through systole and takes longer to shrink to the size at which the leaflets prolapse.

sections.title: Chronic rheumatic heart disease: from repeated carditis to scarred valves

blocks.text: Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis by about 2 to 4 weeks. Antibodies and T cells against streptococcal antigens, particularly M protein, cross-react with cardiac myosin and valve tissue (molecular mimicry), causing a pancarditis with Aschoff bodies and tiny sterile vegetations along the lines of closure (acute disease, Jones criteria, and antistreptolysin O titers in CV-16.2). Chronic rheumatic heart disease is the scar that follows.

A single attack may heal with little damage, but each new streptococcal throat infection can reinflame already scarred valves. Healing replaces inflamed tissue with fibrous tissue and brings new vessels into normally avascular leaflets, so damage accumulates and becomes evident years to decades after the first attack. Rheumatic disease remains the leading cause of MS worldwide, especially where streptococcal pharyngitis goes untreated.

blocks.title: From streptococcal pharyngitis to chronic rheumatic valve disease

blocks.caption: Chronic rheumatic heart disease is the scar of repeated immune injury, not an ongoing valve infection.

blocks.text: Four changes define the chronic lesion: thickened, fibrotic, later calcified leaflets; fused commissures; thickened, shortened, fused chordae; and leaflet neovascularization. Seen from the atrium, the stenotic mitral valve has a rigid fish-mouth or buttonhole orifice, and Aschoff bodies are rarely found because scar has replaced them. Commissural fusion causes stenosis, the signature rheumatic lesion, while retracted leaflets and short chordae prevent closure, so combined stenosis and regurgitation is common. Degenerative disease, by contrast, usually causes isolated AS or isolated MR.

The mitral valve is involved in nearly all cases, alone in about two-thirds and together with the aortic valve in about one-quarter. Tricuspid involvement almost always accompanies left-sided disease, and the pulmonic valve is rarely affected; the usual explanation is that left-sided valves close against systemic pressure and scar more after each episode. Rheumatic aortic disease almost never occurs without mitral disease, so isolated aortic disease in an older adult suggests a calcific or bicuspid valve (section C01). Consequences are those of MS (section C03), plus subacute endocarditis by viridans streptococci (C05) and classic decompensation in pregnancy.

sections.title: Carcinoid heart disease: serotonin and the right-sided valves

blocks.text: Carcinoid tumors are well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors of enterochromaffin cells, most often in the ileum. Many synthesize serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT) from tryptophan through tryptophan hydroxylase and aromatic amino acid decarboxylase, and they also release histamine, kallikrein (which generates bradykinin), tachykinins, and prostaglandins. Monoamine oxidase (MAO) normally converts serotonin to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), which is excreted in the urine.

Gut venous blood passes through the liver, where MAO inactivates these products, so a tumor confined to the bowel usually causes no systemic effects. Liver metastases release products into the hepatic veins and the right atrium, exposing the tricuspid and pulmonic valves first. The lungs protect the left heart, because pulmonary endothelium takes up serotonin through its transporter and degrades it with MAO. Left-sided lesions appear with a patent foramen ovale or other right-to-left shunt, very high levels, or a bronchial carcinoid draining into the pulmonary veins. Ovarian carcinoids, which drain outside the portal system, can cause the syndrome without liver metastases.

blocks.title: Carcinoid heart disease
steps: Serotonin-secreting tumor, often in the ileum
Metastasis to the liver
Serotonin enters hepatic veins, bypassing hepatic MAO
High serotonin reaches the right heart
5-HT2B signaling activates valve interstitial cells
Fibrous plaques on tricuspid and pulmonic valves
Lung MAO lowers serotonin before the left heart
blocks.caption: The portal circulation and the lungs act as two filters, which explains why liver metastases are required and why the left heart is usually spared.

blocks.text: The lesions are pearly white plaques of myofibroblasts in glycosaminoglycan and collagen, laid on right-sided endocardium without destroying the valve beneath. Serotonin acting on 5-HT2B receptors of valve interstitial cells, partly through TGF-beta, drives proliferation and matrix production; 5-HT2B agonists such as fenfluramine and certain ergot-derived dopamine agonists produce similar plaques. Tricuspid leaflets are fixed open, causing tricuspid regurgitation, the most common lesion, and tricuspid stenosis can also occur. Pulmonic cusps thicken and retract, so pulmonic stenosis often coexists with regurgitation, and the right ventricle fails under combined volume and pressure loads.

Kinins, histamine, and tachykinins cause episodic flushing and bronchospasm with wheezing, and serotonin causes watery diarrhea and cramps. Tricuspid regurgitation gives a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration (more venous return to the right heart), with large jugular v waves, a pulsatile liver, edema, and ascites; pulmonic stenosis adds a systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border. Urine 5-HIAA over 24 hours is high, and diversion of tryptophan to serotonin can leave too little for niacin synthesis, causing pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia).

blocks.predict: A patient has a bronchial carcinoid without liver metastases and develops a new valve lesion. Predict which side of the heart is affected.
blocks.explain: The left-sided valves are at risk. A bronchial tumor drains into the pulmonary veins, which carry its products to the LA without passing through the liver or the pulmonary capillary bed where MAO would inactivate them, while the right heart receives systemic venous blood with little serotonin.

blocks.text: Mechanical valves (usually bileaflet pyrolytic carbon) last decades and click crisply, but their foreign surface and abnormal flow make them highly thrombogenic. Bioprosthetic valves are porcine valves or bovine pericardium fixed in glutaraldehyde, which crosslinks collagen, kills the cells, and lowers antigenicity. The tissue is far less thrombogenic but nonviable and unable to repair itself, so structural deterioration commonly occurs within about 10 to 20 years, faster in younger patients. Transcatheter valves are bioprosthetic tissue on a metal frame.

Virchow's triad explains thrombosis: the foreign surface adsorbs plasma proteins and activates platelets and the contact pathway, flow around the hinges creates zones of stasis and high shear, and hypercoagulability or interrupted anticoagulation completes the triad. Mitral prostheses are at greater risk than aortic ones because mitral flow is slower and the LA is often large and fibrillating. Thrombus can immobilize a leaflet (new murmur, muffled clicks, heart failure, shock) or embolize. Pannus is a slower fibrous ingrowth from the sewing ring that narrows the orifice over months to years.

High-velocity turbulent flow fragments red cells, especially through a paravalvular leak (a gap between the sewing ring and the tissue). The intravascular hemolysis gives schistocytes (fragmented red cells, including helmet cells), high lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and unconjugated bilirubin, low or absent haptoglobin, reticulocytosis, and hemoglobinuria. Tubular cells store filtered hemoglobin iron as hemosiderin and shed it, so chronic urinary iron loss can cause iron deficiency. The direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is negative because the destruction is mechanical, and a normal platelet count separates it from DIC, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, and hemolytic uremic syndrome, which also produce schistocytes.

blocks.title: Mechanical hemolysis from a prosthetic valve
steps: High-velocity jet, worst with a paravalvular leak
Shear stress fragments red cells
Schistocytes form; hemoglobin enters plasma
Haptoglobin is depleted; LDH and bilirubin rise
Filtered hemoglobin: hemoglobinuria, hemosiderinuria
Chronic urinary iron loss: iron deficiency
blocks.caption: Each laboratory abnormality marks a step in the destruction of red cells within the circulation.

blocks.text: Bioprosthetic tissue undergoes dystrophic calcification as calcium binds phospholipids of the devitalized cells and altered collagen, faster in children and young adults, and collagen fatigue from repeated flexing adds to it. Cusps stiffen (stenosis) or tear (regurgitation, sometimes sudden).

Prosthetic valve endocarditis begins at the sewing ring and often spreads into the annulus, causing ring abscess, dehiscence, paravalvular leak, and heart block. Early disease (within about the first year, most often the first 2 months) reflects perioperative contamination: coagulase-negative staphylococci, especially Staphylococcus epidermidis, along with S. aureus, gram-negative bacilli, and Candida. This low-virulence skin organism makes a polysaccharide biofilm that binds synthetic material and shields it from neutrophils, complement, and antibiotics; it is a catalase-positive, coagulase-negative, novobiocin-sensitive gram-positive coccus in clusters. Late disease resembles native valve endocarditis.

blocks.title: Complications of prosthetic heart valves
rows: New murmur, muffled clicks, heart failure; stroke or limb infarction
Mechanical, or any valve with a paravalvular leak
Schistocytes, high LDH, low haptoglobin, hemosiderinuria, negative Coombs test
Gradual stenosis, or sudden regurgitation from a cusp tear
Fever, paravalvular regurgitation, ring abscess, heart block; early often S. epidermidis
blocks.caption: Each complication follows from the material, the abnormal flow, or the foreign-body interface.

integration.text: Anatomy and histology show where valve disease begins. Each leaflet is a layered structure of fibrosa, spongiosa, and ventricularis maintained by valve interstitial cells: calcific AS is a disease of those cells turning bone-forming, MVP a disease of excess proteoglycan and weak collagen, rheumatic disease a scar that fuses commissures and shortens chordae, and carcinoid disease a plaque laid on the surface. Chamber relationships explain remote signs, such as an enlarged LA pressing on the esophagus and left recurrent laryngeal nerve, and portal drainage explains why carcinoid tumors need liver metastases.

Physiology supplies the unifying rule: pressure loads produce concentric hypertrophy, volume loads eccentric hypertrophy, and receiving-chamber compliance separates chronic from acute regurgitation. Microbiology and immunology explain the causes (virulence, adhesins, biofilm, molecular mimicry, immune complexes), and coagulation links the sterile lesions and prosthetic thrombosis. Bedside findings have limits: murmur loudness misleads in a failing ventricle, acute regurgitation can be nearly silent, several peripheral signs of endocarditis are nonspecific, and severity thresholds are guideline consensus applied with the whole picture.

summary: Stenosis imposes a pressure load and produces concentric hypertrophy; regurgitation imposes a volume load and produces eccentric hypertrophy.

Calcific AS is an active bone-forming process (earlier on a bicuspid valve) causing a carotid-radiating crescendo-decrescendo murmur, pulsus parvus et tardus, and angina, exertional syncope, and dyspnea.
Chronic AR widens the pulse pressure through a large stroke volume and two-way diastolic runoff; its murmur is early diastolic and decrescendo.
Acute AR and acute MR strike a stiff chamber, so filling pressures rise steeply, edema and shock appear, and the murmur may be short and soft.
Mitral stenosis is almost always rheumatic, loads the LA, lungs, and right heart while sparing the LV, worsens with tachycardia, and a shorter S2 to opening snap interval means higher LA pressure.
Mitral regurgitation gives a holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla and an S3, and the low-pressure LA outlet makes ejection fraction overstate LV function.

Acute endocarditis is usually S. aureus on normal valves, subacute is usually viridans streptococci on damaged valves, and injection drug use favors the tricuspid valve; Janeway lesions are painless and embolic, Osler nodes painful and immune.
NBTE (cancer, hypercoagulability) and Libman-Sacks endocarditis (lupus, either leaflet surface) are sterile and nondestructive, and their main danger is embolism.
MVP is myxomatous degeneration; a smaller LV moves the click earlier and lengthens the murmur. Chronic rheumatic disease fuses commissures and chordae, mainly of the mitral valve.

Carcinoid heart disease needs serotonin to bypass the liver, causes tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonic stenosis, and spares the left heart through lung MAO; prosthetic valves fail by thrombosis, shear hemolysis, tissue degeneration, and endocarditis.

verify: Severity thresholds (AS: valve area about 1 cm2 or less, jet velocity about 4 m/s or more, mean gradient about 40 mmHg or more; MS: valve area about 1.5 cm2 or less) follow current consensus guidelines and have changed over time; confirm the values NABNE expects.

Average survival after symptom onset in AS (about 5 years after angina, 3 after syncope, 2 after heart failure) comes from classic natural history series and is quoted slightly differently between sources.
Prevalence of mitral valve prolapse (about 2 to 3%) and of bicuspid aortic valve (about 1 to 2%) vary with diagnostic criteria and population.
Distribution of chronic rheumatic disease (mitral alone about two-thirds, mitral plus aortic about one-quarter) is from classic pathology series; confirm the figures NABNE uses.
Whether the mitral or the aortic valve is the single most common site of native valve infective endocarditis differs slightly between series; both are cited as the two most common.
The mechanism of Osler nodes (immune complex vasculitis versus microemboli) and of Roth spots is debated; the chapter gives the traditional teaching.
Cutoff for early prosthetic valve endocarditis is given as 2 months in older sources and 1 year in newer definitions.
Durability of bioprosthetic valves (structural deterioration commonly within about 10 to 20 years) varies with valve design, position, and patient age.
Ejection fraction threshold suggesting LV dysfunction in chronic MR (about 60% or less) reflects guideline consensus; the worked example starts above it (65%) to illustrate the principle.

Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms Heyde syndrome, Ortner (cardiovocal) syndrome, Austin Flint murmur, and the named peripheral signs of AR (Corrigan, de Musset, Quincke, Traube, Duroziez), or only the descriptive terms.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: murmur-timing (S1 and S2 with AS, AR, MS, MR, and MVP murmurs drawn on one timeline) and valve-pressure-loops (pressure-volume loops for AS, AR, MS, and MR).
Mitral stenosis heart rate statement (a rise from 70 to 120 per minute roughly doubles the gradient) assumes constant cardiac output and approximate diastolic filling times.
